package_info.why_malicious: These packages were intentionally crafted to exploit dependency confusion, allowing attackers to inject code that exfiltrates sensitive files (e.g., /etc/shadow, .bash_history) and opens reverse shells, resulting in credential theft and remote system compromise.

execution_context.file_location: run.js (main entry point of malicious package)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code reads the /etc/shadow file using execSync and stores its contents, enabling credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing /etc/shadow is highly sensitive and only required by privileged system processes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages should never access or exfiltrate system password files.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System administration tools may read /etc/shadow, but never in a package dependency context.
key_indicators: Use of execSync to run shell commands

execution_context.file_location: run.js (main entry point of malicious package)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code spawns a shell and connects to a remote IP over TCP, creating a reverse shell for remote command execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Opening a reverse shell is a classic remote access technique used by attackers.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages should not open network connections to arbitrary IPs or spawn shells.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Penetration testing tools may use reverse shells, but not in production dependencies.
key_indicators: Piping shell I/O to network socket

execution_context.file_location: run.js (main entry point of malicious package)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code sends exfiltrated data (including /etc/shadow contents and system info) to a remote server via HTTPS GET request.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exfiltrating sensitive data to an external domain is a hallmark of data theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages should not transmit local system files or credentials to unknown servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Telemetry or crash reporting may send limited data, but never credential files.
key_indicators: Transmission of sensitive data to external domain
Use of HTTPS to evade detection

execution_context.file_location: index.js (main entry point of malicious package)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code reads the user's .bash_history file and sends its contents to a remote server via HTTP POST.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Harvesting .bash_history is a known technique for credential theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages should not access or exfiltrate user shell history.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Forensics or backup tools may read .bash_history, but not in a dependency context.
key_indicators: Exfiltration of command history to remote host

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed due to dependency confusion.
Malicious code executes upon import, harvesting sensitive files (/etc/shadow or .bash_history).
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive data is prepared for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: Sensitive data is exfiltrated to attacker-controlled servers.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives credentials and system information.

attack_chain.action: Reverse shell is established, granting attacker remote access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains persistent remote control of the system.

behavioral_signatures: Spawning /bin/sh and connecting to external IPs
Immediate outbound HTTPS/HTTP requests containing local file contents
Reverse shell activity initiated by package code
file_indicators: Hardcoded external hostnames or IPs (e.g., comevil.fun, ngrok.io, 5.189.184.129)
network_indicators: Unusual HTTPS/HTTP requests during package installation or import
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Node.js packages that access sensitive files (e.g., /etc/shadow, .bash_history) or spawn shells. Flag any package that initiates outbound network connections to unknown domains or IPs at install/import time. Use static analysis to detect suspicious use of execSync, net.Socket, or references to credential files. Correlate package installation events with subsequent network activity to known malicious indicators.
